text: In the kickoff, we framed two questions, generated an illustrative messy orders file, audited it, and wrote a cleaning plan. Now we execute — turn that plan into tested code, produce a clean dataset, and answer both questions with real numbers and a chart. Every figure in this lesson comes from our illustrative dataset, generated with seed 42.

Each item in the plan becomes one small function in cleaning dot p-y. Drop underscore duplicate underscore rows just calls drop underscore duplicates. Filter underscore quantity keeps only rows between 1 and a max underscore quantity constant, set to 20 as a business rule you'd confirm with the shop. Clean underscore orders chains every one of these functions together in order with dot-pipe — drop duplicates, standardize text, parse types, filter quantity, handle discount, add revenue.

The date trick is worth calling out on its own. Parse the whole order underscore date column once assuming ISO format, year-month-day, with errors equals coerce, so anything that doesn't match becomes NaT. Parse it again assuming U-S format, month-day-year, the same way. Then fillna combines the two — wherever the ISO parse failed, the U-S parse fills the gap. Every date ends up matching exactly one of the two formats.

Test filter underscore quantity directly — build a tiny Series with a normal value, a zero, a negative number, an absurd 999, and a missing value, and assert only the two reasonable quantities survive, 1 and 5. In total we wrote three tests — date and price parsing, the quantity filter, and checks on the real file itself, asserting unique order IDs, no missing dates, and positive revenue. All three passed.

Load the raw file, run it through clean underscore orders, and print the row count at each stage. 1,530 raw rows become 1,500 once duplicates are dropped, and 1,442 once the quantity rule is applied. Of those, 74 rows have a flagged missing discount. Always report how many rows your cleaning removed — losing about 4 percent of the deduplicated rows to that quantity rule deserves an honest sentence in your write-up, not a silent disappearance.

Filter to completed orders only — 1,267 of them — and sum revenue: about 183,979 dollars total. Group by region and sum revenue, sorted descending, and North leads at about 50,958 dollars, followed by East, West, then South. Group by category instead, and Electronics generates the most revenue, 62,979 dollars, from just 182 orders — because its average order runs about 346 dollars, far above Apparel's 392 orders averaging only 105 dollars each.

So revenue is concentrated in three places. North leads every region, carrying about 51,000 of the full 184,000 dollars. Electronics leads every category despite having the fewest orders, purely on a much higher average order size. And monthly revenue, steady between roughly 10,500 and 15,300 dollars from January through September, jumps sharply to 19,092, then 23,562, then 20,997 in October, November, and December — Q4 alone accounts for 34.6 percent of annual revenue, despite being only 25 percent of the calendar.

Now the discount question. Exclude cancelled orders, cut discount underscore pct into bands — 0 percent, 1 to 10, 11 to 20, and 21 to 30 — then group by band and compute average quantity and return rate together. Average quantity per order stays essentially flat around three items across every single band, so on this data, discounts are not making customers buy more per order. Return rates, though, climb from 7.2 percent at no discount up to 12.6 percent in the highest band. Be careful with the wording here — this shows an association, and that top band has only 103 orders, so treat it as a lead worth testing further, not as proof.

Finally, the chart. Build a bar chart of monthly revenue for completed orders, colored in the brand crimson, titled clearly, and save it to a reports folder at a readable resolution. Because this is code, not a one-off click-through, you can rerun it any time the data changes. The saved chart makes that Q4 surge obvious at a single glance, far faster than reading the raw numbers off a table.

To recap: each cleaning decision became a small, tested function, chained together with dot-pipe. We tracked rows through the funnel the whole way — 1,530, then 1,500, then 1,442. Revenue is concentrated in the North, in Electronics, and in Q4. Discounts didn't raise items per order, and returns ran higher in discounted bands — a lead to investigate carefully, not a conclusion to ship. Next, we wrap up: turning these findings into a presentation and a portfolio piece.
